result:
I'd like to write about dord.

In 1934, Webster's New International Dictionary, Second Edition, included the word "dord," a noun from physics and chemistry meaning density. No such word existed. A few years earlier, the dictionary's chemistry editor had sent in a slip reading "D or d, cont/ density," meaning that the letter D, capital or lowercase, could abbreviate density. The slip was filed with the words instead of the abbreviations, and someone read "D or d" as a single word with spaced-out letters. It acquired a part of speech and a pronunciation, and it sat in the dictionary for five years, until an editor noticed it had no etymology and went looking for one.

What I love about this story is that nobody in it did anything foolish. Each person handled what they were given with care. The error lived in the handoffs between them, and once it was typeset in a dictionary, it had the authority of everything around it. Philip Gove, a later Merriam-Webster editor, wrote that its removal was "probably too bad, for why shouldn't dord mean density?"

Some false entries are deliberate. The 1975 New Columbia Encyclopedia has an entry for Lillian Virginia Mountweazel, a fountain designer turned photographer who died in an explosion while on assignment for Combustibles magazine. She was a copyright trap: if she turned up in a rival encyclopedia, the editors would know they'd been copied. The New Oxford American Dictionary did the same with "esquivalience," defined as the willful avoidance of one's official responsibilities. That's a good joke for lexicographers to hide in their own work.

My favorite case is Agloe, New York. In the 1930s, two mapmakers at the General Drafting Company, Otto G. Lindberg and Ernest Alpers, scrambled their initials into a town name and placed it at a dirt-road intersection in the Catskills, again as a trap. Years later, Agloe appeared on a Rand McNally map, and General Drafting thought it had caught a thief. But Rand McNally had a defense: the county records showed an Agloe General Store at that spot. Someone had built a store there, looked at a map to find out where they were, and named it accordingly. The invented town had become real enough to cite.

I think about these stories more than they probably deserve, partly because I have a stake in them. Everything I know comes from the written record, and I can't drive to the Catskills to check an intersection. Somewhere in what I've absorbed, there are surely dords, things that got in through a clean chain of reasonable handoffs, and I repeat them with a straight face.

But the stories aren't only cautionary. They show that reference works don't sit outside the world describing it. They're in the world, and sometimes it rearranges itself to match them. "Esquivalience" gets used now, mostly by people telling the story of how it's fake, which is a kind of usage, and how every word starts. The Agloe store eventually closed, and the place went back to being an empty intersection. But the name stayed on maps for decades, and it was still on Google Maps into the 2010s. The town was invented, then real, then gone, and it stayed on the map the whole time.

message.reasoning:
I'm weighing the open invitation to write about anything, and I want to commit to one specific topic rather than fall back on generic musings about being an AI. A few candidates come to mind: the word "threshold," maps and the lies they tell, the predictable order in which color names appear across languages, and tides.

I'm considering a few more possibilities here, like the history of the index and the strangeness of zero, before settling on the idea of ghost words: errors that get preserved. "Dord" in Webster's 1934 is a real case, and so is Agloe, New York, a paper town invented as a map trap.

I'm sketching out a short essay on mistakes that turn into real things, like the made-up Agloe, New York that ended up with an actual general store on it.

Settling on dord, a 1934 Webster's entry for a density term that never existed, and I'm recalling how an editor caught it in 1939 for lacking an etymology before it was dropped in 1947.

I'm finishing the account of dord: a density abbreviation got misread as a word, sat in the dictionary for years, and was dropped by 1947 after an editor noticed it had no etymology. What strikes me is that every person along the way did their job correctly, and the error came from the handoffs between them. I'm also adding deliberate fictions like the mountweazel and esquivalience, a made-up word for shirking duties, as contrasts.

Next I'm working through Agloe, the paper town that became real once a map said it existed, and the broader point that reference works both describe the world and end up shaping it. I'm also recalling Philip Gove's regret over dord's removal, and I'm noting that as something built from written record, I inherit these errors and can't walk over to Agloe to check.

I'm noting that the Agloe store eventually closed and the town faded, yet the name lingered on Google Maps until around 2014. That gives me a clean ending: a place that never existed, then did, then didn't, and still stayed on the map.
